questions.stem: Which three parts make one nucleotide?

options.text: A phosphate group, a pentose sugar and a nitrogenous base
options.why: Those are the three parts you need to draw and label. The base is attached to the sugar.

options.text: A phosphate group, an amino acid and a nitrogenous base
options.why: Amino acids build proteins. A nucleotide uses a five-carbon sugar instead.

options.text: A nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a peptide bond
options.why: Peptide bonds link amino acids in proteins. A nucleotide has a phosphate group.

options.text: Two nitrogenous bases linked by a five-carbon sugar
options.why: A nucleotide has one base, one sugar and a phosphate. Paired bases belong to two DNA strands.

questions.stem: Which linkage builds the backbone along one DNA strand?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds between A and T bases on neighboring nucleotides
options.why: Hydrogen bonds pair bases between the two DNA strands. They don't join a strand's backbone.

options.text: Covalent phosphodiester bonds between sugars and phosphate groups
options.why: The alternating sugars and phosphates form a covalent chain. That's one strand's backbone.

options.text: Ionic attractions between charged bases on the same strand
options.why: The bases aren't linked along a strand by ionic attractions. The backbone links sugar and phosphate.

options.text: Peptide bonds between adjacent sugars and nitrogenous bases
options.why: Peptide bonds form in proteins. Nucleotide chains use phosphodiester links in the backbone.

questions.stem: A DNA strand reads 5′-ATGC-3′. What is its complementary strand when written left to right?

options.text: 5′-TACG-3′, because matching strands run in the same direction
options.why: The base letters match, but the direction labels don't. DNA strands run antiparallel.

options.text: 3′-TACG-5′, with opposite strand directions
options.why: T pairs with A, A with T, C with G and G with C. The partner runs 3′ to 5′ left to right.

options.text: 3′-UACG-5′, because uracil pairs with adenine in DNA
options.why: Uracil occurs in RNA. In a DNA partner strand, adenine pairs with thymine.

options.text: 5′-ATGC-3′, because each base pairs with an identical base
options.why: A pairs with T, and G pairs with C. Complementary doesn't mean identical.

questions.stem: Which structural difference identifies ribose rather than deoxyribose?

options.text: It has a phosphate group attached directly to its 2′ carbon
options.why: The 2′ distinction is an OH group, not a phosphate. Phosphate links the sugar backbone.

options.text: It has an OH group on its 2′ carbon instead of an H
options.why: Ribose keeps a 2′ OH. Deoxyribose lacks that oxygen at the same position.

options.text: It has five carbon atoms while deoxyribose has six carbon atoms
options.why: Both are five-carbon sugars. They differ in the group on carbon 2′.

options.text: It contains uracil within its sugar ring rather than thymine
options.why: Uracil and thymine are bases attached to sugars. They aren't atoms within the sugar ring.

questions.stem: Why can one DNA strand specify the base order of a new partner?

options.text: The repeating phosphates determine the identity of every new base
options.why: Phosphates repeat along the backbone and don't carry a changing base-by-base instruction.

options.text: Specific A–T and G–C pairing identifies each complementary base
options.why: Each template base limits which base can pair across from it. That's the basis of copying.

options.text: The strand's histone proteins select bases by matching their shape
options.why: Histones package DNA into nucleosomes. Complementary bases specify the copied sequence.

options.text: Both strands already contain identical bases at every position
options.why: The two strands are complementary, not usually identical. A faces T, and G faces C.

questions.stem: A DNA segment contains 8 positions. How many different base sequences are possible?

options.text: 32, because each of four bases can occupy eight positions once
options.why: A base can appear more than once. Multiplying four by eight misses the independent choices.

options.text: 256, because four base types are paired across two DNA strands
options.why: Pairing determines the opposite strand. It doesn't reduce eight positions to four choices total.

options.text: 65,536, because each of eight positions has four choices
options.why: That's 4^8. The order of bases, rather than a new backbone for each message, creates the variety.

options.text: 40,320, because every base must occur exactly once in the segment
options.why: Bases can repeat. The calculation isn't a permutation of eight distinct items.

questions.stem: What does the near-universality of the genetic code support?

options.text: The idea that all species have exactly the same DNA sequences
options.why: Species differ in DNA sequence. The shared feature is the codon-to-amino-acid correspondence.

options.text: The idea that RNA has replaced DNA as the genetic material of cells
options.why: RNA participates in gene expression, but living cells store hereditary instructions in DNA.

options.text: The idea that all viruses have DNA and must share a common cell ancestor
options.why: Some viruses have RNA genomes. The claim about living organisms doesn't cover every virus.

options.text: Shared codon assignments inherited from a common ancestor
options.why: Nearly the same codons specify the same amino acids across life. A shared origin explains that pattern.

questions.stem: A new RNA chain is being extended during transcription. At which end is the next nucleotide added?

options.text: The 3′ end, leaving the new strand to grow 5′ to 3′
options.why: Nucleotides join to the growing chain's 3′ OH. The template is read in the opposite direction.

options.text: The 5′ end, leaving the new strand to grow 3′ to 5′
options.why: That's backwards for synthesis. RNA polymerase extends the 3′ end of the new strand.

options.text: Either end, depending on whether adenine or guanine comes next
options.why: The base identity doesn't set the growth direction. New nucleotides join at the 3′ end.

options.text: Both ends at once, because the DNA template has two strands
options.why: One RNA strand grows at its 3′ end while a DNA strand acts as the template.

questions.stem: Why do A–T and G–C pairs help keep the DNA helix a consistent width?

options.text: Each pair contains two purines with the same double-ring structure
options.why: A and G are purines, but T and C are pyrimidines. Two purines would make a wider pair.

options.text: Each pair contains two pyrimidines that fit between the backbones
options.why: T and C are pyrimidines, but A and G are purines. Two pyrimidines would make a narrower pair.

options.text: Each pair contains one purine and one pyrimidine
options.why: A–T and G–C occupy similar widths because both pair one purine with one pyrimidine.

options.text: Each pair has the same number of hydrogen bonds between its bases
options.why: A–T and G–C don't have the same number of hydrogen bonds. Their similar width comes from base sizes.

options.text: An RNA strand folded around a single histone protein
options.why: Nucleosomes package DNA, not RNA, and use an eight-histone core.

options.text: A DNA strand wound around a core of eight histones
options.why: DNA winds around the histone core. Linker DNA connects the cores along a longer molecule.

options.text: Two free DNA bases held together by a histone bond
options.why: Bases pair through hydrogen bonds. Histones package DNA at a larger scale.

options.text: An eight-nucleotide sequence enclosed inside one phosphate group
options.why: Phosphates belong to nucleotide backbones. A nucleosome contains a protein core and wrapped DNA.

questions.stem: In Hershey and Chase's experiment, where was most phosphorus-32 found after blending and centrifugation?

options.text: In the supernatant with the sulfur-labeled phage coats
options.why: The supernatant held most protein label. Phosphorus labeled DNA and stayed with infected bacteria.

options.text: In the bacterial pellet, where DNA from the phage had entered
options.why: Phosphorus labeled phage DNA, and most of that label went with the infected bacteria into the pellet.

options.text: Only in newly made viral protein, because phosphorus labels proteins
options.why: Sulfur was used to label protein. Phosphorus labeled the DNA in the original phages.

options.text: Equally in the pellet and supernatant, showing both substances entered
options.why: The two labels separated. Most phosphorus was in the pellet, while most sulfur stayed outside.

questions.stem: One species has 30% A and 20% G in double-stranded DNA. Which values fit Chargaff's findings?

options.text: 30% T and 20% C; other species may have different proportions
options.why: A pairs with T and G with C, so their percentages match within this species. Other species can differ.

options.text: 20% T and 30% C, because purines must pair with identical purines
options.why: A pairs with T and G with C. Purines pair with pyrimidines, not identical purines.

options.text: 25% T and 25% C, because all species must have equal base amounts
options.why: The four bases don't have to be equally abundant. That older fixed-proportion idea didn't fit Chargaff's data.

options.text: 30% C and 20% T, because C is the matching base for A
options.why: C pairs with G, while T pairs with A. Swap those partners back to get the paired proportions.
